title: Blood supply & lymph drainage of the head and neck
blurb: How blood reaches the teeth and drains away, where the lymph nodes are, and why they matter for infection and oral cancer.
question: During an extra-oral examination the dentist feels a hard, painless lump under the jaw on the same side as a long-standing ulcer on the side of the patient's tongue. Why is the dentist checking the neck at all, and why does the type of lump matter?

teach.body: Three systems serve the mouth. Arteries bring oxygenated blood from the heart. Veins carry used blood back. Lymph vessels collect excess tissue fluid, filter it through lymph nodes, and return it to the blood. The nodes are packed with white blood cells, so they swell when they are fighting infection or when cancer cells lodge in them. That is why the dentist feels the neck at every examination.

teach.h: Blood from the heart to a lower tooth

steps.label: Common carotid artery
steps.sub: One each side of the neck

steps.label: External carotid
steps.sub: Supplies the face and mouth (internal carotid goes to the brain)

steps.label: Maxillary artery
steps.sub: Deep to the ramus: supplies the teeth of both jaws

steps.label: Inferior alveolar artery
steps.sub: Runs in the mandibular canal with the nerve

teach.caption: Upper teeth are supplied by the superior alveolar arteries, also branches of the maxillary artery.

teach.h: Key branches of the external carotid artery

children.label: Facial
children.sub: Lips, face; pulse felt at the jaw's lower border

teach.caption: The head and neck have a rich blood supply, which is why the mouth bleeds freely but also heals quickly.

teach.h: Veins: the way back, and a route for infection
teach.body: Veins mostly run alongside the arteries. Blood from the face drains through the facial vein into the internal jugular vein and back to the heart. Deep beside the lateral pterygoid lies a network of veins, the pterygoid plexus; a needle can nick it during an upper molar injection and cause a haematoma (bruise and swelling). Facial veins connect with a venous space behind the eye, the cavernous sinus, so infection around the upper lip and nose can spread inwards. Rare, but serious.

Back of tongue, palate, throat, and the nodes above
teach.caption: Submental and submandibular nodes drain on into the deep cervical chain, so all lymph from the mouth ends up there.

teach.h: The path of lymph from the mouth

steps.label: Tissue fluid
steps.sub: Collected by lymph vessels in the mouth

steps.label: Lymph ducts → veins
steps.sub: Back into the blood at the base of the neck

teach.h: Infection or cancer: how the node feels
teach.body: When a dental abscess or other infection is draining, the nodes in its path become enlarged and tender. Oral cancer spreads (metastasises) through the same lymph vessels, so a cancer on the side of the tongue or floor of the mouth often appears first in the submandibular or deep cervical nodes. A node involved by cancer is typically hard, painless and may feel fixed. The dental nurse records what the dentist finds, and a persistent ulcer with a hard node needs urgent referral.

teach.caption: An ulcer with red and white areas on the side of the tongue. Spread from here would travel first to the submandibular and deep cervical nodes on that side.

teach.text: The INTERNAL carotid supplies the brain and has no branches in the neck; the EXTERNAL carotid supplies the face, teeth and mouth. And a HARD, PAINLESS node is more worrying than a tender one.

items: Heart → aorta → common carotid → external carotid → maxillary artery → alveolar arteries to the teeth.
Face drains via the facial vein to the internal jugular; the pterygoid plexus can bleed during upper molar injections.
Lymph: submental and submandibular nodes → deep cervical nodes → back into the veins.
Tender node: infection. Hard, painless, fixed node: possible cancer spread, so urgent referral.

summary: You can now trace blood from the heart to the teeth, name the key branches of the external carotid artery, explain how the facial veins drain and why infection can spread through them, name the main lymph node groups and what each drains, and tell an infected node from one that may hold cancer.

A.q: Which artery supplies the teeth of both the upper and lower jaws?
A.why: The maxillary artery gives the inferior alveolar artery (lower teeth) and the superior alveolar arteries (upper teeth).

whyNot.0: The facial artery supplies the lips and face.
whyNot.1: The lingual artery supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth.
whyNot.2: The internal carotid supplies the brain and has no branches to the teeth.

A.q: A patient has an abscess on a lower incisor. Which lymph nodes are likely to be tender first?
A.why: The lower incisors drain to the submental nodes under the chin.

whyNot.1: Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp.
whyNot.2: Parotid nodes drain the area around the ear and side of the face.
whyNot.3: Axillary nodes are in the armpit, not the head and neck.

A.q: Which description of a neck lymph node is most suspicious of cancer spread?
options: Tender after a recent sore throat
A.why: A hard, painless node that feels fixed raises concern for metastasis and needs urgent referral.

whyNot.0: Soft, tender, mobile nodes are typical of infection.
whyNot.2: A small node that is settling suggests resolving infection.
whyNot.3: Tenderness after a sore throat points to infection.

B.q: After an upper molar injection, the patient's cheek swells and bruises quickly. Which structure has most likely been nicked?
B.why: The pterygoid plexus of veins lies near the site of an upper molar (posterior superior alveolar) injection and can bleed into the tissues.

whyNot.0: The lingual artery is in the tongue and floor of the mouth.
whyNot.1: The submandibular gland is under the mandible and is not near an upper molar injection.
whyNot.3: The facial nerve is not a blood vessel; affecting it causes weakness, not bruising.

B.q: Where do lymph vessels from the submental and submandibular nodes drain next?
B.why: Both groups drain on to the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.

whyNot.1: Lymph returns to the blood through ducts at the base of the neck, after passing the deep cervical nodes.
whyNot.2: The parotid gland is a salivary gland, not a lymph drainage route for these nodes.
whyNot.3: The maxillary sinus is an air space in the maxilla.

B.q: Which vessel do the facial veins mainly drain into?
B.why: The facial vein joins the internal jugular vein, which returns blood to the heart.

whyNot.0: The external carotid is an artery carrying blood towards the face.
whyNot.2: The maxillary artery carries blood to the teeth, not away from them.
whyNot.3: The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the heart.

C.q: The common carotid artery divides into two. Which branch supplies the face and mouth?
C.why: The external carotid artery supplies the face, teeth, tongue and scalp.

whyNot.0: The internal carotid supplies the brain and eye.
whyNot.1: The vertebral artery supplies the brain via the spine, not the face.
whyNot.2: The subclavian supplies the arm and is not a carotid branch.

C.q: A patient has a long-standing ulcer on the side of the tongue. Which nodes would cancer most likely spread to first?
options: Submental nodes under the chin only
C.why: The side of the tongue drains to the submandibular nodes and on to the deep cervical chain.

whyNot.0: The submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue and the lower incisors.
whyNot.2: These nodes drain the back of the scalp and behind the ear.
whyNot.3: These nodes are in the armpit and groin.

C.q: Why is the dentist careful about infections around the upper lip and nose?
options: They drain to the axillary nodes
Veins there link to the cavernous sinus
The area has no blood supply
The internal carotid runs under the lip
C.why: Facial veins connect with the cavernous sinus behind the eye, so infection can spread inwards.

whyNot.0: This area drains to the submandibular nodes, not the armpit.
whyNot.2: The face has a rich blood supply, which is why it bleeds freely.
whyNot.3: The internal carotid runs deep in the neck and skull, not under the lip.

reteach.title: Roads, drains and checkpoints
reteach.question: Think of the mouth as a town: arteries are the roads in, veins the roads out, and lymph vessels are the drains with checkpoints along the way. What happens at the checkpoints?

blocks.body: Every drain from the mouth passes through checkpoints: the lymph nodes. The first ones are under the chin (submental) and under the jaw (submandibular); all of them feed into the big checkpoint chain running down the side of the neck (deep cervical). When there's trouble upstream, the checkpoint fills with guards (white cells) and swells: tender and sore for an infection. If cancer cells are caught there, they can settle and grow, making the node hard and stuck down. That is why feeling the neck is part of every check-up.

children.label: Submental
children.sub: Lower incisors, tongue tip, mid lower lip

children.label: Submandibular
children.sub: Most teeth and gums, cheeks, side of tongue

blocks.caption: All three end up in the deep cervical chain, then back into the blood.

blocks.text: Sore and soft usually means a fight with infection. Hard, painless and stuck down means the dentist must rule out cancer.

explain.body: Common carotid → external carotid → branches to the face and mouth. The lingual artery feeds the tongue, the facial artery the lips and face, and the maxillary artery the teeth, palate and chewing muscles via the alveolar arteries.

test.q: From which artery does the inferior alveolar artery arise?
test.why: The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of the maxillary artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid.

whyNot.0: The facial artery supplies the lips and face.
whyNot.1: The lingual artery supplies the tongue.
whyNot.3: The internal carotid supplies the brain and has no branches to the teeth.

explain.body: Facial veins drain to the internal jugular vein and the heart. The pterygoid plexus, deep beside the ramus, can bleed after an upper molar injection (haematoma). Facial veins also link to the cavernous sinus, a possible route for infection to spread inwards.

steps.label: Internal jugular vein
steps.sub: Down the side of the neck

test.q: Which complication is linked to the pterygoid venous plexus?
test.why: A needle can pierce the pterygoid plexus during an upper molar injection, causing bleeding into the tissues.

whyNot.0: Dry socket is loss of the clot from an extraction socket.
whyNot.2: A blocked duct involves a salivary gland, not a vein.
whyNot.3: Facial palsy is caused by anaesthetic reaching the facial nerve.

explain.body: Submental nodes under the chin drain the lower incisors and tongue tip. Submandibular nodes under the jaw drain most other teeth, gums, cheeks and the sides of the tongue. Both drain on to the deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein.

explain.caption: Lower incisors drain to the submental nodes; most other teeth drain to the submandibular nodes.

test.q: Which lymph nodes drain the upper molars?
test.why: The upper teeth, and most of the lower teeth, drain to the submandibular nodes.

whyNot.0: Submental nodes drain the lower incisors and tongue tip.
whyNot.1: Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp.
whyNot.3: Parotid nodes drain the region around the ear.

explain.body: Infection makes nodes enlarged and tender, and they settle once it clears. Cancer spreading from the mouth makes nodes hard, painless and sometimes fixed. A persistent mouth lesion with a hard node needs urgent referral.

rows.label: Soft node settling after a cold

test.q: A patient with an ulcer present for five weeks has a hard, painless node under the jaw. What is the correct response by the team?
options: Reassure them it is a cold
Recall them in twelve months to review
test.why: A persistent ulcer with a hard, painless node may be oral cancer that has spread, so it needs urgent referral.

whyNot.0: A hard, painless node with a persistent ulcer should not be dismissed.
whyNot.1: Waiting a year could delay diagnosis of cancer.
whyNot.2: A mouthwash does not address possible malignancy.
